blocks.text: The elements of group 17 (VIIA) of the periodic table are the halogens: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine and tennessine. They are very reactive non-metals, quite similar to one another in chemical properties; the first four are the common members, while astatine and tennessine are very rare and radioactive. The name halogen comes from the Greek 'halos', salt, and 'gen', to make. Chlorine was the first halogen to be isolated and recognised as an element; although poisonous, a small amount is essential to life in the form of chloride.

Halogens exist as diatomic molecules in all phases. Fluorine and chlorine are gases of pale yellow and greenish yellow colour at room temperature and pressure; bromine is a volatile red-brown liquid with corrosive, toxic fumes; iodine is a shiny greyish-black solid that sublimes directly to a violet vapour (Figure 13.1). The colours of the halogens darken progressively from chlorine to iodine, because of changes in the absorption of light by electron transitions within the molecules.
